extracted.intended_audience: fiction writers (beginners) interested in epistolary narrative
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for crafting fiction told through documents (letters, journals, emails, reports, chats, etc.), including voice, tense, pacing, and credibility techniques specific to epistolary narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use appropriate document types
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary writing includes narration through any document (letters, journal entries, emails, newspaper articles, transcripts, police reports, chats, etc.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each type of document has its own tone and style, allowing for creativity and variety; choose a document type that suits the story's needs (e.g., chats for dialogue-heavy stories, journal entries for private contemplation, newspaper articles to flesh out setting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix document forms thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: You can mix multiple document types (letters, diary entries, newspaper clippings, logs) in the same work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mixing is powerful (e.g., Dracula uses letters, diaries, clippings). It helps to find a plausible reason why the documents are assembled (investigation, scrapbook), though readers will often accept an interesting set of documents without an explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know and stick to the document author's voice and audience
rubrics_metrics.description: To write convincing epistolary stories, you must know whom the document’s author is writing to and why, and you must stick to what that writer would say.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the writer deviates from what they'd plausibly say, narration will feel contrived. Consider whether the writer addresses a loved one, a superior, an unknown future reader, etc., and let that choice flavor tone and content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'as you and I both know' exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Sneaking exposition into documents that characters have no reason to state is obvious and tacky—same problem as in bad dialogue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plausible narrative devices (see 'audience' rule) to justify necessary exposition rather than forcing characters to state facts they would not naturally mention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose an audience that justifies needed exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Make the document address someone who legitimately would need background information (e.g., 'whoever reads this' a century later).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A vague future reader can justify detailed explanations (example: The Martian). Alternatively, a specific audience (a loved one) adds flavor and changes tone; use whichever best fits your needs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Motivate omissions and concealed information
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary narration makes it easy to conceal information, but omissions must have a solid character motivation to be believable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an important fact would naturally appear in the kind of document (e.g., a stabbing in a police report), a believable reason is needed for its omission. Remember people simply don't tell each other everything—use that realistically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use tense mixing intentionally
rubrics_metrics.description: Documents can use past, present, or future tense—often mixing them is natural (present for the moment of writing, past to recount events, future for plans).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be thoughtful about mixing tenses so narration stays in sensible order: commonly start in present, go into the past for storytelling, and return to present. Let each document define its own 'present' moment in the timeline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select entry moments to create emphasis and tension
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the points in your story's timeline that will be 'present' for each document to create emphasis, hooks, and suspense.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Have characters write just before something bad or mysterious to hook readers (present tense feels more immediate). Use the time jump at the start of the next document for reveals and teasers. Teasers must be genuine—not deliberately misleading.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accept that epistolary leans toward summary
rubrics_metrics.description: People recount events conversationally and tend to skip minute-by-minute detail; epistolary narration often summarizes rather than scenes everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you need blow-by-blow scenes, provide a realistic reason for such detail (the narrator is excited, a combat enthusiast, writing for someone who wants specifics, or not in a hurry). For short stories, consider narrating a short time span for immersion, but summary can work well for shorter forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specific, visceral details rather than exhaustive listing
rubrics_metrics.description: Include description that feels particular and sensory, but avoid unrealistic exhaustive detail that implies impossible attention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A narrator might note a dusty velvet coat 'like rats had gnawed on it'—such specific image is believable; listing every accessory (hat, hair, eyes, shirt, pants, socks, shoes) without motive will feel implausible and distracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat each document as a one-way conversation
rubrics_metrics.description: Epistolary pieces are dialogue-like: each document functions as a one-way conversation that must feel natural and true to the speaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write documents with the rhythm and naturalness of speech appropriate to the imagined addressee; chats are closest to dialogue, while other forms still need conversational plausibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain genre/form conventions to preserve credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A fiction story that resembles nonfiction documents gains credibility, but only if you rigorously follow the conventions of the chosen document forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adhere to the expected tone, formatting, and rhetorical norms of the form (police report objectivity, newspaper clipping terseness, etc.). This may feel restrictive but increases realism and emotional impact.
